gist: Andy Burnham stated that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum vote.
Burnham gave no details regarding the extent or impact of Moscow's intervention.
Pro-Brexit group Britain Unbound rejected claims that Russian intervention influenced the outcome.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he received a clear answer upon entering Downing Street confirming that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum. He did not reveal who gave the assessment, what evidence was used, or whether it influenced the result. Pro-Brexit group Britain Unbound criticised his remarks, saying there was no good reason to believe Russian intervention influenced the outcome.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Burnham's comments mark the first time a UK prime minister has stated that Russia sought to sway the 2016 vote, departing from previous Conservative positions. Burnham argued that the public had not been sufficiently informed about foreign disruption. He warned that Russian disinformation is also affecting politics in Germany and France, and discussed the issue with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK is strengthening powers under the National Security Act, police, borders, and intelligence agencies. Burnham previously announced a new centre to counter disinformation, and his government will examine all options regarding the UK's future relationship with Brussels.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Steve Jones died at the age of 77. He had a career focused on humanitarian causes, working as an economist and project planner in Bangladesh, India, the Solomon Islands and elsewhere. Later in life, after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis and receiving a lung transplant, he dedicated himself to charity work supporting patients with the disease.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: His work contributed to humanitarian projects, including flood action plans, cyclone recovery and rural poverty reduction. In retirement, he fought on behalf of people with pulmonary fibrosis as chair and patient president of Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis and president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Brooke and Wil lost their baby, Gwilym Ioan, last December. Despite raising concerns about his health, they were told he was fine. Medical records later indicated a serious neonatal infection. Ten months later, the couple are still awaiting a report, a post-mortem examination, and an inquest into his death.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Families in Wales report that investigation processes are often defensive and inconsistent, causing further trauma. Bereaved parents frequently struggle to access information or support, leading some to campaign for systemic changes to maternity services and bereavement care.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: An inquest into Gwilym's death is ongoing. Meanwhile, the Welsh government is considering calls for national targets to reduce neonatal and stillbirth rates and is working to implement bereavement care pathways across health boards.

gist: Specialist endometriosis centres face losing accreditation without increased funding, dedicated teams and adequate theatre capacity.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Kelly O'Shea woke from operations to discover her endometriosis surgery was not done because a bowel surgeon was unavailable or theatre time ran out. Specialist centres in Wales face losing accreditation from the British Society for Gynaecological Endoscopy due to severe resource challenges, funding differences with England, and a lack of dedicated multidisciplinary team time.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Without proper resources, Welsh specialist centres risk downgrading services, losing skilled staff, and sending large numbers of patients to England for care at a higher cost. Clinicians warn that women are left in chronic pain, accumulating scar tissue from incomplete procedures, and waiting years for treatment.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Discussions are underway to establish a regional or national service through the NHS Wales joint commissioning committee or an overhaul of the funding model. Health boards are working towards reaccreditation, and a petition regarding the Cardiff and Vale centre has gathered over 11,000 signatures.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: About 650 offenders serving sentences of up to two and a half years are leaving jails in England and Wales. Under the government's scheme, prisoners are released after serving one third of their term rather than half, following an earlier release of 700 offenders on 1 October.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The releases are intended to tackle the prison population crisis. However, probation union Napo stated that the policy places enormous strain on staff tasked with community monitoring. Probation officers may hold a strike ballot after rejecting a 5% pay offer from the Ministry of Justice.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Batches of prisoners with increasingly long sentences will be freed, finishing next June with those serving over 12 years. The government is also returning court reform proposals to Parliament, including expanding magistrate sentencing powers to two years and piloting virtual hearings directly from police cells.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham reopened the Brexit debate in the House of Commons, arguing that leaving the European Union has caused more harm than good. He indicated that Labour's next manifesto might promise an in-out referendum. Burnham also claimed he received a clear answer confirming Russian interference in the 2016 referendum, though Boris Johnson disputed this by stating there was no evidence of successful interference.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Burnham hopes closer ties with Brussels will boost economic growth and curb illegal immigration, while attracting pro-European left-wing voters. However, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued this risks repeating old arguments with little success, and former negotiator Lord Frost asserted politicians owe voters a defence of the 2016 decision.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A merchant ship sank and another was hit after drones struck two vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast. One ship went down east of Krapets with one crew member saved, while a Ukrainian-owned vessel was hit near Byala with all 15 crew rescued. Prime Minister Rumen Radev summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova, noting logic suggests the outcome benefits Russia.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated the Black Sea is becoming another front of escalation in the Russian war. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the attack demonstrates Moscow's disregard for civilian lives and maritime security, warning that Russia is attacking global food security to weaponise hunger.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he would speak shortly to Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte following the emergency meeting.

sections.text: Artificial intelligence labs and tech companies are purchasing code and workspace archives from struggling or defunct startups. sections.text: Training laboratories need new material because they have exhausted standard public and synthetic datasets. However, legal experts warn that selling employee messages and emails creates privacy risks since workers usually do not share in the profits or give explicit consent.

timeline.text: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?

gist: Scientists used computer-generated audio to revive a 1960s sparrow song in Buenos Aires.
Learning traditional songs helps birds attract mates and successfully defend their territory.
Researchers suggest AI and live tutors could aid conservation by teaching lost songs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Researchers created a computer-generated rendition of a rufous-collared sparrow song from the 1960s that had disappeared from a Buenos Aires park. Less than three months after playing it, a local bird began to copy parts of the tune. In another project, translocated cirl buntings initially produced abnormal songs before returning to normal over several years.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Birdsong is an essential part of animal culture and population health. Birds that sing well in a familiar dialect are better placed to find mates, defend territory and survive. Population declines and human encroachment can cause songs to change or disappear, threatening breeding success.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Scientists hope synthetic recordings and AI could help teach birdsong to dwindling or endangered species where real-life recordings do not exist. Researchers continue to register dialects and communication systematically.

fivew: Researchers including Gabriel B Mindlin, Rebecca Lewis and Sarah Collins.
Scientists used computer-generated audio and tutors to help birds learn lost songs.
Decades after the songs disappeared in the 1960s.
A park in Buenos Aires and other locations.
To help birds improve breeding success and aid conservation efforts.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Gwent Police launched eleven murder probes in ten months, leading to high overtime and reduced community policing. Separately, Chicago police used DNA evidence to identify a former homicide detective as the killer of an eight-year-old girl from a 1960 cold case.

sections.heading: Why it matters

gist: English cathedrals face severe financial crises and structural decay despite their cultural importance.
Most cathedrals lack secure state funding and face significant maintenance cost burdens.
The decline of cathedrals threatens the future of English choral music traditions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: English cathedrals are experiencing a financial crisis, with 80% currently in structural deficit. Despite high visitor numbers and their role as community hubs, many buildings are deteriorating. Some institutions have begun charging for entry and hosting events like silent discos to diversify income, yet financial instability persists.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Cathedrals serve as vital centres for community life, local identity, and historical connection. They provide essential musical training and educational opportunities for children. Because they lack secure state funding and VAT exemptions on repairs, their physical decline directly endangers the survival of English choral music.

Local representatives and religious leaders have expressed deep sorrow, while the Justice Minister condemned the act as brutal and heinous, promising that those responsible will face the law.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A senior investigating officer is leading the murder inquiry from an incident room at Waterford Garda Station. Forensic experts are examining the crime scene, and post-mortem examinations are scheduled. Gardaí are appealing for witnesses and dashcam footage from the area between 04:30 and 05:30 on Tuesday.

gist: Google allows US users to launch personal, vibe-coded Android apps privately via Google Play.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Google announced that US users aged 18 and older can now launch vibe-coded personal apps directly on their Android devices via Google Play. Using standard Google accounts, creators can run custom applications built with Google AI Studio without connecting to a computer or publishing publicly.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Previously, running native Android creations often required publishing to Google Play's wider audience, driving many creators towards web apps. Google keeps these private apps out of public search listings, positioning the system as a stepping stone for new developers.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: In the coming months, Google will allow users to share their vibe-coded creations with trusted friends. Creators will also be able to graduate apps to public listings after passing Trust & Safety reviews.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of rapper Tupac Shakur. sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: OpenAI sacked and reported engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, after discovering an encrypted recording device wrapped in toilet paper plugged into a television USB port inside an executive conference room. BBC News reported the device was in San Francisco, whereas The Guardian noted OpenAI did not disclose the specific office. OpenAI said it used AI models to trace the device to Alfozan, who was subsequently arrested and federally charged.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The FBI alleged the goal was capturing sensitive communications regarding the firm's AI product. OpenAI stated there was no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were improperly accessed or exfiltrated, framing the incident as proof of AI aiding defences against insider risks and sophisticated threats.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Alfozan appeared in federal court on Tuesday after being held in custody. OpenAI confirmed the FBI's investigation is ongoing, and the firm stated it will continue supporting their work.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Intense wildfires driven by an El Nino climate phenomenon have triggered toxic smog across Indonesia, Singapore, and Malaysia. Over one million wildfire hotspots burned thousands of hectares of land through slash and burn practices.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Hazardous air quality has raised public health concerns, forcing school closures and leaving residents short of breath. Authorities face mounting pressure as activists and officials clash over corporate accountability and cross-border environmental impacts.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Researchers at UCL and Tohoku University studied how Japanese speakers learn English. They found that learners with high auditory precision master pronunciation faster by processing foreign sounds as non-speech. It challenges the idea that some nationalities are inherently poor at languages, pointing instead to insufficient exposure and ineffective teaching methods that neglect essential listening training.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Machine translation usage has grown rapidly, with Google Translate alone processing one trillion words monthly. sections.text: In low-stakes scenarios, raw AI output is often sufficient. Because modern AI output sounds natural, human reviewers may overlook dangerous inaccuracies that were previously obvious in clunky machine translations.

gist: English and Welsh water firms could return £107m via lower bills after missing targets.
Yorkshire Water and Thames Water face multi-million pound penalties from regulator Ofwat.
Severn Trent and Northumbrian Water could receive reward payments resulting in higher bills.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Ofwat estimated that several water providers, including Yorkshire Water and Thames Water, missed performance targets and must return tens of millions of pounds through lower bills. Overall, the industry faces a net reduction of £240m for failures during 2025-26, with £107m expected to be returned to customers in 2027-28. Conversely, firms like Severn Trent and Northumbrian Water met their targets and are in line for reward payments covered by higher bills.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The privatised water industry faces intense scrutiny over sewage pollution, high debt, and underinvestment. Because customers cannot switch providers, Ofwat uses automatic penalties and rewards based on performance targets. These financial pressures arrive as the government considers bringing debt-laden firms like Thames Water under public control and aims to protect households from rising costs.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Ofwat's current figures remain at the draft stage. The regulator will make its final decision on the penalty and reward payments by 15 December, and the changes will take effect on customer bills starting from 1 April 2027.

articles.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
articles.standfirst: Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol.

timeline.text: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision

gist: Astronomers used NASA’s Chandra observatory to explain the Treble Clef radio wave formation.
The structure was likely caused by a black hole outburst and galaxy cluster collision.
Researchers published their findings in the Astronomy & Astrophysics journal on Wednesday.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Astronomers used NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory and other telescopes to investigate a radio wave formation nicknamed the Treble Clef, hidden behind the Milky Way. They determined it is hosted by two merging galaxy clusters and likely formed in a two-stage process involving a supermassive black hole outburst followed by a cluster collision.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The discovery explains a formation that was previously difficult to understand because intervening stars, gas, and dust from the Milky Way block the view from Earth, revealing how black hole outbursts and cluster collisions interact.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A writer used a personalized health program that builds a virtual model of a person using daily biometric inputs, blood tests, and wearable devices. After logging numerous meals, measurements, and activity levels over three months, follow-up lab tests revealed notable improvements in liver enzymes and triglycerides.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Digital twins represent a growing trend in personalized medicine, aiming to help individuals manage chronic health issues and predict treatment responses. While low-stakes metabolic coaching shows promising results, the technology demands significant personal data and ongoing tracking from the user, raising questions about privacy and data fatigue.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The author decided to continue using the digital twin program for another three months with slightly more flexibility regarding data logging. Meanwhile, researchers continue to explore the broader applications and challenges of digital twins in higher-stakes medical fields such as cancer care.

gist: UK airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed after rising sharply.
The RAC welcomed the review, citing driver anger over escalating fees.
Airports defended the charges as necessary to manage traffic and emissions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government confirmed a review of airport drop-off charges following analysis showing average prices at major airports rose by a third since the summer of 2025. Gatwick and Stansted increased from £7 to £10, Edinburgh from £6 to £8.50, and Bournemouth, Leeds Bradford and London City to £8. Belfast International increased to £5.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Department for Transport stated the review is vital to ensure fair treatment and accessible travel. The RAC argued the fees frustrate drivers, while Airports UK stated the charges manage traffic, reduce pollution, and compensate for a lack of state subsidies compared to EU airports.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The government will carry out the review of airport drop-off fees.

gist: Apate uses AI agents to bait fraudsters and gather intelligence.
The startup has wasted years of scammer time and raised funds.
Clients include major banks and telecommunications companies.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Australian startup Apate deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims to bait fraudsters across calls, messages, email, and social media. Founded in 2024 based on research at Macquarie University, the company raised $8.15 million in seed funding in August and recently pitched at TechCrunch Disrupt.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The undercover agents waste scammers' time and trick them into revealing bank accounts, crypto wallets, and other details. This intelligence helps clients like Commonwealth Bank of Australia and TPG Telecom inform their anti-fraud measures, with Commonwealth seeing a drop in publicly reported scam losses.

fivew: An Australian startup deploys undercover AI agents to bait scammers and gather fraud intelligence.
To waste scammers' time and gather useful intelligence for banks and telecom companies.

timeline.text: Saracens sack academy player Auvaa after latest incident
Two punch-ups, two red cards, no chances left - Saracens sack Auvaa

gist: Saracens have sacked Totoa Auvaa following an investigation into a recent altercation.
The club dismissed the player after multiple off-field and on-field disciplinary issues.
Auvaa previously received support from the club after an incident involving England cricketers.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Saracens terminated Totoa Auvaa's contract following reports of a punch-up in St Albans. The club conducted an internal investigation and reached a decision within four hours. This followed a history of disciplinary concerns, including two red cards for violent conduct while on loan at Ampthill.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The club stated they had obligations to their supporters, partners, and young people. While teammates previously defended Auvaa citing his youth and distance from home, the club ultimately decided his behaviour was unacceptable and that his development was not progressing sufficiently.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Auvaa is now a free agent. While he may seek opportunities with other European clubs, potential employers will likely scrutinise his disciplinary record before offering a contract.

fivew: Saracens sacked player Totoa Auvaa following an investigation into a punch-up.
The club announced the sacking on a Monday afternoon.
The incident occurred in St Albans.
The club cited a series of off-field and on-field disciplinary issues.

gist: Manchester City's rule breaking may have cost other Premier League teams up to £844m.
The financial impact includes missed Champions League qualification, lower prize money, and relegation costs.
Tottenham, Hull City, and Everton were among the most financially impacted clubs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Manchester City faced charges related to inflating sponsorship income and expenses between 2009 and 2018. BBC Sport calculated that thirty-five other top-flight clubs were left financially out of pocket due to missed prize money, relegation costs, and missed European qualification.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The financial impact on other clubs is calculated at £844m, affecting league placing money, relegation costs, and missed Champions League and Europa League earnings. Tottenham suffered a net loss of £119.9m, Hull City faced £99m in relegation-related costs, and Everton experienced a combined impact of £66.4m.

gist: Millwall manager Neil criticised for comments regarding a match stoppage over alleged racial abuse.
Referee Edward Duckworth paused the match after being alerted to accusations and spoke with officials.
Kick It Out expressed disappointment over reports of racist abuse directed towards Eom.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Referee Edward Duckworth paused a match at The Den following accusations of racist chants. An announcement was made over the speakers regarding the alleged abuse and police use of CCTV. Millwall manager Neil criticised the stoppage, stating he wanted the game restarted because the issue would be dealt with after the event anyway. Both clubs condemned the incident, while Kick It Out expressed disappointment over reports of racist abuse towards Eom.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Kick It Out stated that protocols ensure players are protected and key details are captured for accountability, regardless of how long it takes. Millwall and match officials were praised for following the right protocols.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Saracens sacked 21-year-old academy player Totoa Auvaa with immediate effect following an incident in St Albans on Saturday. Auvaa had previously been involved in a June nightclub incident in London involving England cricketers Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson, where a member of security was struck.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Saracens stated that Auvaa's conduct fell short of the standards expected of everyone representing the club. The club emphasised its commitment to upholding standards for supporters, young people and partners.

gist: San Francisco beat Seattle 32-29 to go 5-0 in week five.
Minnesota moved to 5-0 after a defensive win against New Orleans.
Washington and the New York Giants played out a 27-27 tie.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: San Francisco defeated Seattle 32-29 in a brutal divisional contest. The Minnesota Vikings beat the New Orleans Saints 23-13. The Washington Commanders and New York Giants finished in a 27-27 tie after late errors by both teams. The Baltimore Ravens beat the Atlanta Falcons 30-23 in overtime, and the New York Jets defeated the Cleveland Browns 17-12.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: San Francisco and Minnesota both reached 5-0 records, placing them among the standout teams of the early season. The 49ers showed their potential Super Bowl capabilities, while defensive masterclasses shaped several results across the league.

gist: Lisandro Martinez criticised Manchester United's board for failing to strengthen the squad.
Former players Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young suggested the comments could damage team unity.
Manager Michael Carrick stated he needs to investigate the situation before taking action.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: After a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid, defender Lisandro Martinez publicly criticised Manchester United's hierarchy for insufficient investment in the squad. He specifically questioned the technical director, Jason Wilcox, and suggested the club failed to build a strong enough team following their Champions League qualification. The club has struggled recently, failing to win in five matches.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The comments have sparked debate regarding player conduct and club management. Former players Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young argued the public criticism was disrespectful to teammates and could harm dressing room morale. Conversely, some observers and fans feel Martinez's honesty reflects long-standing concerns about recruitment and ownership decisions under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Omar Berrada.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Manager Michael Carrick, who has not yet seen the full interview, indicated he would address the matter after gathering more information. The club faces ongoing pressure regarding its recruitment strategy, financial debt, and the performance of the current squad.

gist: Celtic beat Motherwell 2-0 to return to the Scottish Premiership summit.

The victory helped lift recent gloom following three straight defeats.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Celtic returned to winning ways by beating Motherwell 2-0 at Fir Park, with goals from Camilo Duran and Benjamin Nygren. The victory moved Martin O'Neill's side back to the Scottish Premiership summit following three straight defeats. Winger Jota also made his long-awaited return from injury as a substitute after almost 18 months on the sidelines.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The win provided welcome cheer for a disgruntled fanbase and lifted the recent gloom surrounding the club. It eases the pressure on manager Martin O'Neill, who had previously questioned whether he had the energy to continue following defeats against Rangers.

fivew: Celtic beat Motherwell 2-0 and returned to the Scottish Premiership summit.
To bounce back from three straight defeats and lift recent club gloom.
